title: Calcium carbonate in northern shrimp side streams impedes growth and development of Hermetia illucens (Diptera : Stratiomyidae)
content:
Abstract
Worldwide population growth has increased the need for sustainable waste management within food systems. Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) can upcycle various organic residues into protein- and lipid-rich biomass. Shrimp side streams are produced in massive quantities, remain underutilized, and could be valorized this way. This project aimed to evaluate the impacts of shrimp coproducts and CaCO3 on bioconversion and development. We hypothesized that increasing Ca concentrations would impede growth and bioconversion and delay development. A control diet (Gainesville, 70% relative humidity) was compared to 9 diets with increasing levels of Ca (3.3%, 4.3%, and 8.3% Ca, dry basis) through partial substitution with hydrolyzed or non-hydrolyzed shrimp powder (10%, 20%, and 40%, dry basis), or CaCO3 (4%, 8 and 16%, dry basis) through feeding trials (3 trials; 2 repetitions/diet) using BSFL (4 days post-hatching; feeding rate of 30 mg/individual/day, dry basis). All Ca-enriched diets caused Ca accumulation in larvae, with the highest levels caused by diets containing 8.3% Ca. Bioconversion was decreased by diets containing 4.3% and 8.3% Ca from CaCO3 and 8.3% Ca from raw and hydrolyzed shrimp powder. The diet containing 8.3% CaCO3 also resulted in delayed adult emergence. In this study, increased levels of Ca in the diets resulted in increased Ca bioaccumulation in larvae. High concentrations of Ca (8.3%) negatively impacted growth and delayed development. Side stream combinations and chelating agents could decrease calcium to tolerable levels, allowing the upcycling of high-calcium side streams into calcium-enriched BSFL.
